title: Scarce clinic time and opportunity cost — Arden
stem: All places, agents and data in this question are constructed for practice. In Arden, a local clinic has 30 staff-hours available on a Saturday. One screening uses 2 staff-hours and one home visit uses 3. All staff-hours are fully usable for either service.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define scarcity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum number of screenings if no home visits are offered.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the opportunity cost of allocating 6 staff-hours to home visits instead of screenings.

steps.text: Resources are limited relative to the wants they could satisfy.
Consequently choices between competing uses are necessary; a shortage at one price alone is not the definition.
Maximum screenings = 30/2.
15 screenings.
Six hours permit two home visits.
The same hours could provide three screenings.
The opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone: three screenings.
The monetary wage bill need not change; the forgone service is still a cost.

title: Classifying productive resources — Doreva
stem:
All places, agents and data in this question are constructed for practice. In Doreva, a workshop uses a leased building, a forest parcel, trained carpenters and a founder who coordinates production and bears commercial risk.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: The building is bought second-hand.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the factor of production represented by the forest parcel and explain why.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish the building from the carpenters as factors of production.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the founder's entrepreneurial role and one associated opportunity cost.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: Land.
It is a natural resource rather than a produced input.
The produced building is capital used to make other output.
The carpenters supply labour: human effort and skills.
The founder organizes the factors of production.
The founder makes decisions under uncertainty and bears risk.
For example, the founder forgoes a salaried management job.
That next best alternative income is an opportunity cost even if it is not an accounting payment.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
It remains produced capital; being previously owned does not turn it into land. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

title: Increasing opportunity cost on a frontier — Gavela
stem:
All places, agents and data in this question are constructed for practice. In Gavela, a repair centre can produce the following combinations using all its current resources.

| Combination | Bicycles repaired | Radios repaired |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 60 |
| B | 10 | 54 |
| C | 20 | 42 |
| D | 30 | 24 |

No technical change occurs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the opportunity cost in radios of moving from B to C.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the opportunity cost per bicycle from C to D.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why these data are consistent with a bowed-out PPC.

steps.text: Radios forgone = 54 − 42.
12 radios.
1.80 radios per bicycle.
The sacrifice for ten extra bicycles rises from 6 to 12 to 18 radios.
Thus marginal opportunity cost rises as bicycle repairs expand.
Some tools and skills suit radio repair better than bicycle repair.
Reallocation increasingly uses less suitable resources; this generates the bowed-out frontier.

title: Recovery within an unchanged PPC — Merin
stem:

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

Some available resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
Actual growth raises realized output, for example by using idle machines.
